en.statement: When an image reference has a tag and a digest, the kubelet uses the tag to choose the image.
en.explanation: The kubelet pulls the image identified by the digest when a reference includes both a tag and a digest.

en.statement: Pinning a Deployment's image by digest keeps its new Pods on that image when a registry tag moves.
en.explanation: An image digest identifies fixed content. Moving a registry tag leaves the content selected by the Deployment's digest unchanged.

en.statement: For a newly created Pod using `:latest`, Kubernetes defaults an omitted imagePullPolicy to Always.
en.explanation: At creation, the API server assigns Always when the image uses the latest tag and imagePullPolicy is omitted.

en.statement: Changing a Deployment's image tag to `:latest` automatically changes its imagePullPolicy to Always.
en.explanation: Kubernetes sets the default imagePullPolicy at object creation. A later image change preserves the existing policy unless you explicitly edit it.

en.statement: A Pod's imagePullSecrets can reference a registry credential Secret stored in a different namespace.
en.explanation: A Pod's imagePullSecrets refer to Secrets in that Pod's namespace. Create the registry credential Secret in the namespace that uses it.

source.title: Pull an Image from a Private Registry

en.statement: A ServiceAccount's imagePullSecrets automatically populate new Pods that use it and omit imagePullSecrets.
en.explanation: The ServiceAccount admission controller copies the ServiceAccount's imagePullSecrets into a new Pod whose spec lists none, so the Pod can pull from that private registry.

en.statement: Setting a container's args alone makes the kubelet replace the image's default executable command.
en.explanation: When you supply args and leave command unset, the kubelet runs the image's default command with your replacement arguments.

source.title: Define a Command and Arguments for a Container

en.statement: The API server can accept changes to each container's command when you update an existing Pod.
en.explanation: A container's command is fixed when the Pod is created. Create a replacement Pod to use a different command.

source.title: Define a Command and Arguments for a Container

en.statement: The kubelet expands `$(VAR)` in container args using the container's environment variables.
en.explanation: The kubelet substitutes a defined environment variable in a command or argument that uses the $(VAR) form.

source.title: Define a Command and Arguments for a Container

en.statement: A StatefulSet controller automatically creates the headless Service named in its manifest.
en.explanation: You create the headless Service used for a StatefulSet's network identity; the StatefulSet controller does not create it.

en.statement: A StatefulSet keeps its template-created PersistentVolumeClaims after scale-down by default.
en.explanation: StatefulSet retention defaults to Retain, so template-created PersistentVolumeClaims survive scale-down.

en.statement: A DaemonSet controller automatically adds a Pod when a newly joined node meets its scheduling constraints.
en.explanation: A DaemonSet controller reconciles newly added eligible nodes by creating a Pod there.

en.statement: A Job's `parallelism` sets the total number of successful Pods needed for each completed Job.
en.explanation: A Job's parallelism controls concurrent execution. For a fixed-completion Job, completions sets the success count.

en.statement: A Job's `activeDeadlineSeconds` stops retries even when its `backoffLimit` still permits them.
en.explanation: A Job stops launching retries when its active deadline expires, even if its retry allowance remains.

en.statement: Setting a Job's `suspend` to true pauses its active Pods so they resume from their current processes.
en.explanation: Suspending a Job terminates its active Pods; resuming creates replacement Pods rather than continuing their paused processes.

en.statement: Under its default success rules, an Indexed Job waits for a successful Pod at each completion index.
en.explanation: Under its default success rules, an Indexed Job counts multiple successful Pods with the same index as one completed index.

en.statement: A CronJob with `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid` replaces its active Job when the next scheduled run is due.
en.explanation: With Forbid, a CronJob skips a scheduled run while its previous Job remains active, instead of replacing that Job.

en.statement: By default, a CronJob interprets its schedule in the worker node's local time zone.
en.explanation: The kube-controller-manager uses its own local time zone for a CronJob schedule when timeZone is omitted.

en.statement: Two containers in one Pod can reach each other's network listeners through the shared localhost address.
en.explanation: Containers in one Pod use the same network namespace, so localhost reaches listeners in a sibling container.

en.statement: The kubelet can run ordinary init containers concurrently before starting the app containers.
en.explanation: The kubelet runs ordinary init containers in sequence, waiting for one to succeed before it starts the next.

en.statement: By default, containers in one Pod see one another's processes through a shared process namespace.
en.explanation: Containers use separate process namespaces by default. Set shareProcessNamespace to true when containers need to inspect one another's processes.

en.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.33, a running native sidecar holds a Job open after its main containers finish.
en.explanation: A native sidecar's continued execution does not block its Job from completing after the main container finishes.

en.statement: A container restart preserves the files stored in its Pod's emptyDir volume.
en.explanation: The kubelet keeps an emptyDir volume across container restarts within the same Pod.

en.statement: A container's writes to a memory-backed emptyDir count toward its ephemeral-storage limit.
en.explanation: Files written to a memory-backed emptyDir count against the memory limit of the container that wrote them.

en.statement: The control plane creates a generic ephemeral volume's PersistentVolumeClaim from the Pod's template.
en.explanation: For a generic ephemeral volume, the ephemeral volume controller creates the PersistentVolumeClaim using the Pod's volumeClaimTemplate.

en.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.36, a runtime with image volume support mounts an image volume read-only.
en.explanation: The runtime exposes an image volume's OCI image or artifact as read-only content for mounted files.

en.statement: A ReadWriteOnce volume can accept read-write mounts from multiple Pods on the same node.
en.explanation: ReadWriteOnce restricts read-write mounting to one node, so Pods sharing that node can use the same volume.

en.statement: Setting a PersistentVolumeClaim's `storageClassName` to an empty string selects the default StorageClass.
en.explanation: An empty storageClassName requests storage with no class. Omitting the field permits default StorageClass selection.

en.statement: Scaling a Deployment with `kubectl scale` makes its controller record a new rollout revision.
en.explanation: A Deployment records a revision for a Pod template change. Changing the desired replica count leaves its rollout revision unchanged.

en.statement: You can change an existing Deployment's label selector through `kubectl apply` with an updated manifest.
en.explanation: The API server rejects changes to an existing Deployment's label selector. Changing that selector requires replacing the Deployment.

en.statement: For a rolling update, maxSurge sets how many desired replicas the Deployment controller can leave unavailable.
en.explanation: maxSurge gives a rolling update room to create Pods above the desired replica count.

en.statement: `kubectl rollout status` exits with a non-zero code once a Deployment exceeds its progress deadline.
en.explanation: When a Deployment passes its progressDeadlineSeconds, rollout status prints an error and returns a non-zero exit code, so a script or pipeline can detect the stalled rollout.

en.statement: `kubectl rollout undo` can restore a Deployment's Pod template from a particular retained revision.
en.explanation: kubectl rollout undo accepts a chosen revision from the retained rollout history, allowing recovery to an earlier Pod template.

en.statement: `kubectl rollout pause` makes the Deployment controller stop the containers in its running Pods.
en.explanation: Pausing a Deployment holds back rollouts from Pod template updates. Existing Pods keep running while the Deployment is paused.

en.statement: The Deployment controller automatically rolls back a stalled rollout when progressDeadlineSeconds expires.
en.explanation: The controller reports Progressing=False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded after the deadline. Kubernetes reports the stall and leaves rollback to you or another orchestrator.

en.statement: You can switch blue/green traffic between two Deployments by changing the frontend Service's selector.
en.explanation: A frontend Service selects the active version's Pods. Switching that selector directs new traffic to the other prepared Deployment.

source.title: Zero-downtime Deployment in Kubernetes with Jenkins

en.statement: With default Service routing to both versions, canary traffic roughly follows the ready Pod replica ratio.
en.explanation: With a Service balancing across ready Pods from both Deployments, adjusting their replica ratio changes the approximate canary traffic share.

source.title: Deploy a Release Using a Canary Deployment

en.statement: `helm rollback` restores the target's earlier revision number as the current number.
en.explanation: A Helm rollback creates a new revision containing the target revision's configuration. Its revision number increases instead of returning to the target number.

en.statement: Helm gives `--set` values precedence over conflicting settings in `--values` files.
en.explanation: Values supplied with --set override conflicting settings in --values files during the same install or upgrade.

en.statement: Helm gives the first `--values` file priority when several files override the same value.
en.explanation: When several --values files define the same setting, Helm takes the value from the rightmost file.

en.statement: `helm upgrade --reset-values` clears the release's previously stored `--set` values.
en.explanation: Helm stores --set overrides with a release. An upgrade using --reset-values discards those saved overrides and starts from the chart's defaults.

en.statement: `helm uninstall` retains a release's history by default after deleting its resources.
en.explanation: Helm uninstall deletes the release history by default. Adding --keep-history retains that record after the resources are removed.

en.statement: `helm template` renders chart manifests locally by default for review before release installation.
en.explanation: Helm template displays rendered Kubernetes manifests for inspection. The command leaves installation to a separate step.

en.statement: `helm search repo` can search Artifact Hub before its repositories are added locally.
en.explanation: Helm search repo searches the chart repositories added to the local Helm client. It reads their locally cached indexes.

en.statement: `helm install` accepts a chart reference from an OCI registry as its installation source.
en.explanation: Helm install accepts OCI chart references. This uses an OCI registry as the chart source instead of a traditional chart repository.

en.statement: Helm 4's first upgrade of a Helm 3 release uses server-side apply by default.
en.explanation: When Helm 4 first upgrades a Helm 3 release, it keeps client-side apply by default. An explicit --server-side override changes the method.

en.statement: `kubectl kustomize` can apply its rendered resources to the current cluster as part of the same command.
en.explanation: kubectl kustomize prints the rendered resources. Use kubectl apply -k to apply the kustomization to the cluster.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

en.statement: Several Kustomize overlays can list one base directory under resources, each building its own variant of that base.
en.explanation: A base has no knowledge of its overlays, so one base can serve dev and prod overlays that each add their own patches or name prefix while the base itself stays unchanged.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

en.statement: By default, Kustomize changes a generated ConfigMap's name when configMapGenerator content changes.
en.explanation: Kustomize appends a content hash to generated ConfigMap names. Changed input produces a different suffix, and Kustomize updates references to the generated name.

source.title: Declarative Management of Kubernetes Objects Using Kustomize

en.statement: Kustomize selects patch targets satisfying either the name or labelSelector when both are supplied.
en.explanation: A Kustomize patch target combines its selection criteria. A resource must match both the supplied name and labelSelector for that patch to apply.

en.statement: Kustomize's namespace field leaves a namespaced resource's explicitly assigned namespace unchanged.
en.explanation: The namespace transformer sets the namespace on namespaced resources, overriding namespace values already present in those resources.

en.statement: By default, Kustomize automatically includes generated ConfigMaps when it applies namePrefix.
en.explanation: The namePrefix transformation covers generated resources as well as resources loaded from manifests. A generated ConfigMap therefore receives the configured prefix.

en.statement: The patches field accepts strategic merge patches and JSON 6902 patches in the same kustomization.
en.explanation: Kustomize's patches list supports both patch formats. Entries may load a patch file or contain an inline patch.

en.statement: When two patches set the same scalar field, Kustomize keeps the value from the earlier patch in the list.
en.explanation: Kustomize applies patches in their listed order. A later patch that sets the same scalar field replaces the value left by an earlier patch.

en.statement: Kustomize automatically adds labels from the labels field to Deployment selectors by default.
en.explanation: The labels field leaves selectors unchanged unless includeSelectors is true. Its default behavior adds the labels to resource metadata.

en.statement: Kubernetes keeps deprecated GA API versions available within the same major version.
en.explanation: A GA API version can be deprecated while Kubernetes continues serving it within the same major version. Deprecation alone does not authorize its removal.

en.statement: Kubernetes counts a beta API version's removal grace period from its original introduction.
en.explanation: The beta removal window starts at deprecation. Kubernetes serves the version for at least nine months or three minor releases after that, whichever lasts longer.

en.statement: Kubernetes gives alpha API versions the same advance removal notice as beta API versions.
en.explanation: An upgrade can drop an alpha API endpoint even when the previous release gives no warning that the endpoint will disappear.

en.statement: Once a cluster stops serving autoscaling/v2beta2, clients read existing HorizontalPodAutoscalers through autoscaling/v2.
en.explanation: For each removed API version, the migration guide states that existing persisted objects are accessible via the new API. Only manifests and clients that still name the old version need updating.

en.statement: By default, `kubectl apply` returns an error when the API server warns about a deprecated API.
en.explanation: kubectl apply prints server warnings and completes an otherwise successful request by default. Treating warnings as command errors requires opting into that behavior.

en.statement: `kubectl explain` describes fields using the OpenAPI schema it fetches from the cluster's API server.
en.explanation: kubectl explain retrieves field information from the server in OpenAPI format, so its output reflects the API versions that cluster serves; --api-version picks a specific group/version.

en.statement: A fresh installation of the official kubectl binary includes the `kubectl convert` plugin.
en.explanation: kubectl convert is distributed as a separate plugin binary. Install it separately before using it to migrate manifests between API versions.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

en.statement: Kubernetes v1.37 accepts new CronJobs submitted with `apiVersion: batch/v1beta1`.
en.explanation: Use batch/v1 for current CronJob manifests. Kubernetes stopped serving the batch/v1beta1 CronJob endpoint in v1.25.

en.statement: With the Metrics Server installed, Kubernetes v1.37 clients reach metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1 after the API's v1 graduation.
en.explanation: The metrics.k8s.io API graduated to v1 in Kubernetes v1.37, and v1beta1 remains usable throughout the transition under the API deprecation policy, so existing clients keep working.

en.statement: The kubelet counts an exec probe as successful when the probe command exits with status zero.
en.explanation: For an exec probe, the command's exit status determines the check result; zero signals success.

en.statement: A TCP probe succeeds when the application accepts the connection and immediately closes it.
en.explanation: A TCP probe checks whether it establishes a connection, even if the application immediately closes that connection.

en.statement: A gRPC probe can invoke a custom RPC method named in the Pod manifest.
en.explanation: Kubernetes gRPC probes call the standard gRPC Health Checking Protocol rather than a chosen application RPC method.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

en.statement: The kubelet automatically waits for a startup probe to succeed before liveness or readiness probes run.
en.explanation: A successful startup probe releases the gate that delays the container's liveness and readiness checks.

en.statement: The kubelet waits for a readiness probe to succeed before beginning the container's liveness checks.
en.explanation: Liveness checks run independently of readiness results; an unsuccessful readiness probe does not hold them back.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

en.statement: Once a readiness probe has succeeded, the kubelet stops running it for that container.
en.explanation: The kubelet keeps running readiness probes throughout a container's lifetime, checking for changes after initial success.

source.title: Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes

en.statement: An aggressive liveness probe can increase load on surviving Pods by restarting overloaded containers.
en.explanation: Probe-triggered restarts reduce serving capacity during overload, shifting work to remaining Pods and potentially causing further probe failures.

en.statement: The API server accepts a readiness probe with its own `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` value.
en.explanation: The API server rejects terminationGracePeriodSeconds in readiness probes because readiness failure leaves the container running.

en.statement: The API server rejects an ordinary init container that defines a `startupProbe`.
en.explanation: Ordinary init containers do not support startupProbe, so the API server rejects that probe configuration.

en.statement: By default, `kubectl logs deployment/web` prints the logs of a single Pod that belongs to that Deployment.
en.explanation: For a workload such as a Deployment or Job, kubectl logs reads one of its Pods. Add --all-pods to fetch logs from every Pod, which also prefixes each line with its source.

en.statement: `kubectl logs --previous` on a replacement Pod can retrieve logs from the old Pod it replaces.
en.explanation: The --previous option retrieves the preceding instance of a container in the same Pod, if that instance exists. It does not retrieve logs from a replacement Pod's predecessor.

en.statement: `kubectl logs` with a label selector matches labels on Deployment objects to choose Pods.
en.explanation: A label selector supplied to kubectl logs selects Pods by their own labels. Labels on a Deployment object do not determine this selection.

en.statement: `kubectl logs` can combine a container's latest log file with older rotated files retained on its node.
en.explanation: kubectl logs exposes the latest log file for the selected container instance. Older rotated files can remain on the node but are excluded from that response.

en.statement: `kubectl cp` automatically uses the target container's tar executable to transfer files.
en.explanation: kubectl cp runs tar inside the target container during file transfers. The operation fails when that executable is unavailable there.

en.statement: The API server rejects CPU requests declared through resources on an ephemeral debugging container.
en.explanation: Ephemeral containers disallow the resources field, so they cannot declare CPU requests even though regular containers accept them.

en.statement: The kubelet automatically restarts a crashed ephemeral container in a Pod with `restartPolicy: Always`.
en.explanation: The kubelet leaves a terminated ephemeral container stopped, regardless of the Pod's restartPolicy. Its debugging session ends when its process exits.

en.statement: Given `--container`, `kubectl debug --copy-to` can change that container's command in the copied Pod.
en.explanation: kubectl debug can create a Pod copy with a changed command for the named container. Omitting --container instead adds a new container to run the supplied command.

en.statement: With FallbackToLogsOnError, the kubelet replaces existing termination message text with log output.
en.explanation: With terminationMessagePolicy set to FallbackToLogsOnError, the kubelet uses log output when the termination message file is empty and the container exits with an error.

source.title: Determine the Reason for Pod Failure

en.statement: A CustomResourceDefinition's `spec.scope: Namespaced` lets you put that definition object inside a namespace.
en.explanation: A CustomResourceDefinition is cluster-scoped. Its spec.scope field determines the scope of the custom resource instances, rather than the CRD object.

source.title: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

en.statement: By default, the API server removes unknown fields from custom resources before it stores accepted objects.
en.explanation: The API server removes fields absent from a custom resource's structural schema. A schema can opt specific subtrees out of this pruning.

source.title: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

en.statement: By default, recreating a deleted CustomResourceDefinition restores the custom objects previously stored through it.
en.explanation: Deleting a CustomResourceDefinition deletes its stored custom resource objects. Recreating the same CRD starts with an empty collection.

source.title: Extend the Kubernetes API with CustomResourceDefinitions

en.statement: Once its CustomResourceDefinition exists, a new Database custom resource makes the control plane start database Pods.
en.explanation: On its own, a custom resource only stores and serves structured data. Database Pods start only when a custom controller, such as an operator, watches those objects and creates the workloads.

en.statement: A narrower RoleBinding removes permissions that the same user receives from a broader RoleBinding.
en.explanation: RBAC combines permissions from applicable bindings. Adding a binding with fewer permissions leaves grants from other bindings in effect.

en.statement: A RoleBinding lets you reuse a ClusterRole to grant a ServiceAccount Pod access within the binding's namespace.
en.explanation: A RoleBinding references a ClusterRole to reuse its rules for namespaced resources. The binding grants those permissions within its own namespace.

en.statement: Validating admission controllers receive a Pod with labels already added by mutating admission controllers.
en.explanation: The API server runs validation after the mutation phase. Validating admission evaluates the object with mutations already applied.

en.statement: Admission controllers can reject a `kubectl get` request based on the requested object's field values.
en.explanation: Read requests bypass admission control. Admission rules therefore do not reject kubectl get requests based on the retrieved object's contents.

en.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.36, the API server evaluates MutatingAdmissionPolicy CEL expressions in its own process.
en.explanation: MutatingAdmissionPolicy evaluates CEL inside the API server, providing admission mutations without an external webhook service.

en.statement: When a container's CPU request differs from its limit, the scheduler uses its limit to check node capacity.
en.explanation: The scheduler uses CPU requests to decide whether a node has enough CPU available for a Pod. Limits are not its CPU placement budget.

source.title: Assign CPU Resources to Containers and Pods

en.statement: The kernel throttles CPU time when a container's workload tries to exceed its CPU limit.
en.explanation: Linux enforces a container's CPU limit through throttling, restricting the CPU time available to that container.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

en.statement: The kernel may OOM-kill a container whose memory consumption exceeds its memory limit.
en.explanation: Memory limit enforcement is reactive: the kernel can kill a container under memory pressure after it exceeds its limit.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

en.statement: By default, Kubernetes uses a container's CPU limit as its CPU request when admission leaves the request unset.
en.explanation: If admission supplies no default CPU request, Kubernetes copies the container's specified CPU limit into its request.

source.title: Resource Management for Pods and Containers

en.statement: By default, the admission controller applies updated LimitRange defaults to existing Pods.
en.explanation: LimitRange defaulting happens during admission. Updating its defaults leaves the resource settings of existing Pods unchanged.

en.statement: Kubernetes rejects a Pod whose container CPU limit exceeds its namespace LimitRange's CPU maximum.
en.explanation: A LimitRange max constrains each container's CPU limit, so a create request for a Pod over that maximum fails at the API server with HTTP status 403 Forbidden.

en.statement: A requests.cpu ResourceQuota permits creation of Pods that omit both CPU requests and CPU limits.
en.explanation: A requests.cpu ResourceQuota rejects a new Pod with no CPU request or limit when admission supplies no defaults. Omitting the fields does not bypass the quota.

en.statement: After you lower a requests.cpu ResourceQuota below existing usage, the control plane evicts Pods to meet it.
en.explanation: Lowering a CPU ResourceQuota leaves existing Pods running even if their total requests exceed the new budget. The new quota governs subsequent admission.

en.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.35, the kubelet can replace a Pod to apply a memory resize using `RestartContainer`.
en.explanation: A memory resize with RestartContainer restarts the affected container inside the same Pod. The resize preserves the Pod's identity.

source.title: Resize CPU and Memory Resources assigned to Containers

en.statement: A container can use valueFrom to map one ConfigMap key to an environment variable with a different name.
en.explanation: An env entry with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef selects a named ConfigMap key. The entry's name determines the environment variable name.

en.statement: A running container keeps its existing ConfigMap-derived environment values when the ConfigMap changes.
en.explanation: The kubelet reads ConfigMap values when it starts the container. Restart the container to load changed values into its environment.

en.statement: After the ConfigMap changes, the kubelet refreshes a file from it that a container mounts with subPath.
en.explanation: A ConfigMap file mounted with subPath stays on its original contents. Updates to the ConfigMap do not propagate through that mount.

en.statement: The kubelet may expose image files at a volume's mount path when its optional ConfigMap source is missing.
en.explanation: The kubelet still creates the optional ConfigMap volume's mount path. A missing ConfigMap leaves that mounted volume empty.

source.title: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

en.statement: The kubelet automatically retries startup when a Pod's container references a missing required Secret.
en.explanation: A missing required Secret leaves the affected container waiting. The kubelet retries and reports an Event until it can obtain the Secret.

en.statement: Once a ConfigMap's immutable field is true, a patch setting it back to false fails at the API server.
en.explanation: Once immutable is true, the API server rejects reverting it and any change to data or binaryData. To change contents, delete and recreate the ConfigMap, then recreate the Pods that use it.

en.statement: The API server accepts plain text values in a Secret's stringData field when creating the Secret.
en.explanation: The stringData field accepts unencoded strings as Secret input. The API server converts those values into stored data entries.

en.statement: The API server verifies that a kubernetes.io/tls Secret's certificate matches its private key.
en.explanation: For a kubernetes.io/tls Secret, the API server checks for tls.crt and tls.key but does not validate their values.

en.statement: `kubectl create configmap` imports files from nested subdirectories when its source is a directory.
en.explanation: Directory import reads regular files immediately inside the chosen directory. kubectl skips nested directories and other non-regular entries.

source.title: Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap

en.statement: By default, a Pod in namespace apps with serviceAccountName unset uses the default ServiceAccount in namespace default.
en.explanation: When serviceAccountName is unset, Kubernetes assigns the ServiceAccount named default in the Pod's own namespace. A Pod in apps uses apps' default ServiceAccount.

en.statement: Once a Pod exists, an update that changes its serviceAccountName fails API server validation.
en.explanation: A Pod's serviceAccountName can be set only at creation or in a template for new Pods. Create a replacement Pod to assign a different ServiceAccount.

en.statement: A ServiceAccount's automountServiceAccountToken setting takes precedence over the Pod's setting.
en.explanation: When both a Pod and its ServiceAccount set automountServiceAccountToken, the Pod's value controls automatic credential mounting for that Pod.

en.statement: By default, the kubelet automatically rotates a projected ServiceAccount token before the token expires.
en.explanation: The kubelet requests a replacement as the projected token approaches expiration. The application needs to reload the token file to use the replacement.

en.statement: When runAsUser differs, the container's securityContext overrides the Pod's configured user ID.
en.explanation: The runtime uses the container's runAsUser value when the Pod and container both specify it. The container-level value takes precedence for that container.

source.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

en.statement: With runAsNonRoot true, the kubelet automatically selects a nonzero UID for an image configured as root.
en.explanation: runAsNonRoot makes the kubelet check the container's user and refuse startup if it would run as UID zero. The setting does not choose a replacement UID.

en.statement: With readOnlyRootFilesystem true, the runtime also makes a container's mounted volumes read-only.
en.explanation: readOnlyRootFilesystem affects the container's root filesystem. Mounted volumes retain their own read/write settings, independent of that root filesystem setting.

source.title: Configure a Security Context for a Pod or Container

en.statement: A Pod's securityContext supports capabilities settings that apply across its containers.
en.explanation: Configure capabilities in each individual container's securityContext. PodSecurityContext does not provide a capabilities field for a Pod-wide setting.

en.statement: A runtime upgrade can change the syscall filter a Pod receives with seccompProfile.type set to RuntimeDefault.
en.explanation: RuntimeDefault uses the container runtime's built-in profile. That profile can differ across runtime versions, so the field does not pin a fixed syscall allow-list.

source.title: Restrict a Container's Syscalls with seccomp

en.statement: Since Kubernetes v1.36, with supporting kernels and runtimes, hostUsers false maps Pod UID zero to a non-root host UID.
en.explanation: Setting hostUsers to false puts the Pod in a user namespace. The kubelet chooses a host mapping that lets root inside the container remain unprivileged on the host.

en.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, a new namespace's Pods permit incoming TCP traffic by default.
en.explanation: Pods start open to incoming connections in a namespace that has no NetworkPolicies. Installing an enforcing plugin does not itself isolate them.

en.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, a Pod's ingress allowance can come from either of two matching policies.
en.explanation: NetworkPolicies selecting a Pod combine their ingress allowances instead of intersecting them.

en.statement: For new TCP connections, a NetworkPolicy-enforcing plugin lets destination ingress override blocked source egress.
en.explanation: A new Pod-to-Pod connection needs permission for source egress and destination ingress. Permission at the destination does not override blocked source egress.

en.statement: A NetworkPolicy's empty podSelector includes Pods with unrelated labels in that policy's namespace.
en.explanation: An empty podSelector matches Pods throughout the policy's own namespace, regardless of their labels.

en.statement: By default, a NetworkPolicy that defines egress rules and omits policyTypes applies to egress alone.
en.explanation: Kubernetes defaults policyTypes to include Ingress and adds Egress when the NetworkPolicy defines egress rules.

en.statement: In a NetworkPolicy, namespaceSelector and podSelector as separate from items admit sources matching either.
en.explanation: Elements of a from list are ORed: the podSelector element admits matching Pods in the policy's namespace, and the namespaceSelector element admits all Pods in matching namespaces. In one element they combine as AND.

en.statement: The Kubernetes documentation recommends NetworkPolicy ipBlock for allowing traffic from specific in-cluster Pod IPs.
en.explanation: ipBlock CIDRs should be cluster-external IPs, because Pod IPs are ephemeral and unpredictable. Select in-cluster Pods with podSelector and namespaceSelector instead.

en.statement: A NetworkPolicy with endPort uses a named port as the start of its destination port range.
en.explanation: A NetworkPolicy port range needs a numeric port value. The API server rejects endPort combined with a named port.

en.statement: With a plugin enforcing NetworkPolicy, ingress isolation still permits traffic from the Pod's own node.
en.explanation: NetworkPolicy leaves connections from a Pod's resident node permitted, even when its ingress rules grant no access.

en.statement: Changing a Pod's labels can move it into the backend set of an existing Service.
en.explanation: The control plane watches for Pods matching the Service's selector and updates its backend set when their labels change.

en.statement: When port and targetPort differ, clients connect to targetPort on the Service's cluster IP.
en.explanation: Clients connect to the Service's port on its cluster IP. The Service forwards that traffic to the backend's targetPort.

en.statement: A Service's named targetPort reaches Pods that use different port numbers for the same port name.
en.explanation: The Service resolves the named targetPort against each selected Pod's declared port. Matching port names can therefore refer to different numbers.

en.statement: You link a manual EndpointSlice to a selectorless Service by giving the slice an owner reference to that Service.
en.explanation: You link an EndpointSlice to a Service by setting the kubernetes.io/service-name label on the slice. An owner reference records ownership and does not choose the Service.

en.statement: With cluster DNS installed, a headless Service with a selector returns ready Pod IPs in DNS lookups by default.
en.explanation: A headless Service's DNS records point to its backing Pods rather than a virtual cluster IP, so the client receives endpoint addresses.

en.statement: With cluster DNS installed, a Pod's short Service name lookup searches across namespaces by default.
en.explanation: A short Service name uses the querying Pod's namespace. To look up a Service in another namespace, include that namespace in the DNS name.

en.statement: For application Services, the kubelet limits Service environment variable discovery to the Pod's namespace.
en.explanation: The kubelet supplies environment variables for application Services in the Pod's own namespace. Services in another namespace do not contribute those variables.

en.statement: For a Service backed by several Pods, `kubectl port-forward` can balance local connections across those Pods.
en.explanation: kubectl port-forward selects one matching Pod and forwards the session to it. It does not use Service load balancing across the backend set.

en.statement: The EndpointSlice controller keeps an empty slice for a Service whose selector matches zero Pods.
en.explanation: With zero selected Pods, the EndpointSlice controller preserves an empty placeholder slice. Its endpoints list contains no Pod addresses.

en.statement: The API server can accept valid Ingress objects before an administrator installs an Ingress controller.
en.explanation: Creating an Ingress records routing configuration. An Ingress controller needs to implement that configuration before it affects traffic.

en.statement: With a single default IngressClass, the API server assigns it when a new Ingress leaves its class unspecified.
en.explanation: DefaultIngressClass admission assigns the single default class during Ingress creation. The new object's ingressClassName receives that class's name.

en.statement: For Ingress TLS to work, each host in the tls section has to match a host in the rules section.
en.explanation: TLS does not work on the default rule, which names no host, since its certificate would have to cover every possible subdomain. So hosts in the tls section need to explicitly match rule hosts.

en.statement: An Ingress controller ignores letter case when it compares a request path with an Exact path such as `/docs`.
en.explanation: Exact path matching is case-sensitive, so a rule with the Exact path /docs does not match a request for /Docs.

en.statement: An Ingress controller treats the request path `/api-v2` as matching a Prefix path configured as `/api`.
en.explanation: Ingress Prefix compares complete slash-separated elements; api-v2 is a different element from api.

en.statement: A pathType of ImplementationSpecific lets an Ingress rule use regular-expression syntax defined by Kubernetes.
en.explanation: ImplementationSpecific gives the selected Ingress controller control over path interpretation. Kubernetes leaves those matching semantics to that implementation.

en.statement: An Ingress controller prefers `/api/v2` over `/api` when both Prefix paths in one Ingress match a request.
en.explanation: When Ingress paths match the same request, the longest path takes precedence; /api/v2 outranks /api.

en.statement: In the Ingress specification, defaultBackend handles requests whose selected Service has zero Pods.
en.explanation: Ingress defaultBackend covers unmatched requests. A matched rule keeps its backend selection even when that Service has zero Pods.

en.statement: The standard Ingress TLS model sends the client's encrypted TLS session onward to the Service backend.
en.explanation: Ingress TLS assumes termination at the Ingress entry point. The documented model sends plaintext traffic from there to the backend Service.
